What the comparison tells us

The original model reduced fluctuations, but earned less

Across these 27 development decisions, the S&P 500 portfolio delivered the highest return. The original three-asset model had the lowest volatility, but its lower return outweighed that reduction in risk.

S&P 500: highest growth, largest swings

100% SPY earned 11.9% annualized and 28.7% cumulatively. It also had the highest volatility (19.5%) and the deepest peak-to-trough loss (−23.9%).

60/40: a middle ground

The fixed mix earned 4.3% annualized and 9.9% cumulatively, with lower volatility than SPY alone. Its −20.5% drawdown was the smallest of the three.

Original model: less volatility, weaker results

The model earned 1.1% annualized and 2.4% cumulatively. Volatility was lowest at 12.5%, but its −21.1% drawdown was slightly worse than 60/40. Its Sharpe of 0.08 was also the lowest.

What this means for the MVP: The model did not outperform either fixed portfolio in this development sample. It reduced volatility, but the results do not yet show that its forecasts and allocation changes added value.

How to read the metrics

Annual return is the compounded growth rate expressed per year. Cumulative return is the total gain across the sample. Volatility measures how much monthly returns fluctuate, expressed annually. Max drawdown is the largest observed fall from a previous portfolio peak. Sharpe compares return with volatility; higher is better. Here it uses annualized return divided by annualized volatility and assumes a zero cash rate.

This development sample is short. Results describe this period; they do not establish future outperformance.

Subsequent outcome

The original model, explained

How the starting mix becomes a decision

The original three assets stay the same. Their weights change as the model combines economic news, forecasts, and risk.

1. Start with 45 / 35 / 20

45% SPY holds U.S. equities. 35% IEF holds 7–10 year U.S. Treasuries. 20% LQD holds investment-grade corporate bonds. This neutral mix anchors Black–Litterman.

2. Summarize the news

Payrolls, retail sales, industrial production, and ISM form the Growth surprise. CPI, Core CPI, PPI, and hourly earnings form the Inflation surprise. Each group averages its available standardized surprises.

3. Forecast each asset

Ridge estimates next-month returns for SPY, IEF, and LQD using earlier data. Shrinkage limits extreme forecasts. Policy expectations, financial conditions (ANFCI), and geopolitical risk (GPR) add context.

4. Blend and allocate

Black–Litterman combines the starting mix’s implied returns with Ridge forecasts. The optimizer then balances expected return, risk, and turnover within allocation limits.

Black–Litterman after Ridge

Starting mix + model views + uncertainty → moderated returns

Prior (π)

The neutral return estimate implied by the 45 / 35 / 20 starting mix and asset covariance.

Views (Q)

The three Ridge return forecasts. The replay above shows each raw view alongside its BL result.

Covariance (Σ)

Capital sigma: how asset returns move together, estimated from up to 36 earlier months.

Uncertainty (Ω)

Capital omega: each view’s earlier forecast-error variance. Higher uncertainty reduces the view’s influence.

Allocation limits: SPY 20–70%, IEF 15–60%, LQD 10–40%. Weights sum to 100%. The 60/40 and SPY-only reference portfolios keep their fixed allocations.

Data and limits

What is in the updated MVP

Macro releases

Eight Bloomberg release and consensus series from the Oct 26 workbook. Surprise scaling uses prior observations only.

Risk context

Chicago Fed ANFCI and Caldara–Iacoviello GPR. Both use latest revised history, not a locked real-time vintage.

Asset returns

SPY, IEF, and LQD adjusted-close returns. ETF history in the current source begins in October 2016.

Policy history

The workbook’s 3-month and 6-month implied policy paths begin in September 2019. Earlier missing policy fields use past-only median imputation inside Ridge.
